Received 11 December 2024 l Revised 27 January 2025 l Accepted 27 January 2025 l Published online 10 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: The malnutrition screening tool (MST) has been widely validated for detecting malnutrition in various countries. However, its applicability in Thai outpatient settings remains unexplored. This study aimed to translate the MST into Thai and assess its validity and reliability compared to the global leadership initiative on malnutrition (GLIM) criteria. Material and Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital, including 248 participants. Nutritional status was evaluated using the Thai-translated MST (T-MST), mini nutritional assessment-short form (MNA- SF), and GLIM criteria, which included bioelectrical impedance analysis for muscle mass assessment. Sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating charateristic curve (ROC-AUC), test-retest reliability, inter-rater reliability, and internal consistency (item-total score correlation and Cronbach’s alpha) were analyzed to assess the MST’s performance relative to the GLIM criteria. Results: The Thai version of the MST demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC]=0.976, p-value<0.001) and inter-rater reliability (ICC=0.917, p-value<0.001). It showed strong agreement with the GLIM criteria (Kappa=0.843), comparable to the MNA-SF (Kappa=0.834). Internal consistency was satisfactory (Cronbach’s alpha=0.794). The T-MST achieved a sensitivity of 86.5% and specificity of 96.0%, while the MNA-SF showed a sensitivity of 93.2% and specificity of 93.1% against the GLIM criteria. Both tools demonstrated excellent predictive accuracy (ROC-AUC: T-MST=0.907, MNA-SF=0.929). Conclusion: The T-MST is a reliable and efficient tool for malnutrition screening in outpatient settings. Its simplicity and ease of use make it particularly valuable in time-constrained environments. However, ongoing validation across diverse populations and settings is essential to ensure consistent performance across different clinical contexts. JSON: Name: thai_mst_glim_validation Title: Cross-sectional diagnostic validation of a Thai-translated Malnutrition Screening Tool (T-MST) against GLIM criteria in adult outpatient clinics Short Hypothesis: The Thai-translated Malnutrition Screening Tool (T-MST) will detect GLIM-defined malnutrition with sensitivity ≥85% and specificity ≥90% in adult outpatient populations. Related Work: Existing work has validated the Malnutrition Screening Tool (MST) in multiple clinical contexts (acute care, rehabilitation, oncology, outpatient clinics) showing generally high inter-rater and test-retest reliability and variable diagnostic accuracy versus subjective global assessment tools. Other short instruments such as the MNA-SF have been validated for older adults and often show higher sensitivity but require more items and anthropometric inputs. Prior studies commonly used the Subjective Global Assessment (SGA) or clinical judgement as the reference standard, introducing subjectivity and between-study variability. Limitations in prior work include inconsistent reference standards, reduced sensitivity in certain disease-specific cohorts (e.g., renal patients), sparse validations of translated versions in non-English settings, limited use of objective muscle-mass measures (BIA or DXA) in outpatient validations, and limited generalizability due to convenience sampling and small subgroup sizes. Abstract: This research pipeline defines a cross-sectional diagnostic validation of a Thai-translated Malnutrition Screening Tool (T-MST) using the GLIM criteria with objective muscle-mass measurement as the reference standard in adult outpatient clinics. The protocol includes forward-backward translation, cognitive pilot testing, standardized rater training, and blinded concurrent administration of T-MST, MNA-SF, and GLIM (including BIA). Primary contribution is a rigorous, reproducible evaluation framework quantifying diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, ROC-AUC), reliability (inter-rater ICC, test-retest ICC), and internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha) of the T-MST, plus prespecified subgroup and ablation analyses (replacement of BIA with calf circumference). Expected outcome is demonstration of the T-MST’s accuracy and operational reliability for rapid outpatient screening and specification of contexts where the T-MST performance diverges from broader instruments or GLIM diagnostics. Experiments: Design: prospective cross-sectional diagnostic study. Population and datasets: consecutive adult outpatients (age ≥18) attending internal medicine and family medicine clinics at one tertiary hospital; target N=300 (expected malnutrition prevalence 25–35%, yielding ~75–105 GLIM-positive cases). Translation: forward-backward translation by bilingual clinicians and linguists; pilot N=20 for comprehension. Measurements: all participants receive (1) T-MST administered by rater A, (2) MNA-SF administered by rater B, (3) GLIM diagnostic assessment by blinded assessor C including BIA-derived appendicular skeletal muscle index (ASMI) with thresholds men<7.0 kg/m2, women<5.7 kg/m2. Reliability subsets: randomly selected n=60 for inter-rater (two independent raters within same visit) and n=60 for test-retest (same rater, 7±2 days). Ablation/comparison arms: (A) GLIM-BIA reference vs GLIM-calffold (calf circumference) reference (same participants); (B) T-MST cutpoint sensitivity analysis (>=2 vs alternative cutpoints). Baselines: MNA-SF classification and GLIM reference. Metrics: sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV with 95% CI; ROC-AUC and DeLong test for AUC differences; Cohen’s kappa for categorical agreement; ICC (two-way random, absolute agreement) for inter-rater and test-retest with 95% CI; Cronbach’s alpha and item-total correlations; McNemar test for paired sensitivity/specificity comparisons; subgroup ROC and logistic regression for age (>=65), cancer, respiratory and GI disease groups. Statistical thresholds: two-sided alpha=0.05. Sample-size justification: N=300 chosen to obtain at least 75 GLIM-positive cases to estimate sensitivity 0.85 with ±0.08 precision (95% CI). Data handling: exclude participants with incomplete primary measures; perform missing-data sensitivity using multiple imputation if <10% missing. Analysis software: R or SPSS; report point estimates and 95% CIs. Risk Factors and Limitations: Translation risk: semantic differences may alter item interpretation and affect validity. Self-report bias: inaccurate recall of weight loss or appetite changes may affect sensitivity. Reference-standard dependence: GLIM requires BIA; BIA device variability and technique errors can bias muscle-mass classification. Sampling bias: single-center outpatient recruitment and convenience/consecutive sampling may limit generalizability to other regions, inpatient settings, or non-Thai speakers. Prevalence dependence: PPV and NPV will vary with malnutrition prevalence, limiting direct transfer of predictive values. Subgroup power: limited sample sizes in diagnostic subgroups (e.g., cancer, COPD) may yield imprecise estimates. Cross-sectional design: cannot assess temporal predictive validity or clinical outcomes. Operational scalability: BIA availability and trained personnel requirements restrict feasibility in resource-limited clinics. Statistical risks: spectrum bias and verification bias if reference assessments are not uniformly performed or if excluded participants are non-random.
